title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
statement: You get a binary search tree and two values p and q that are both in it. Return the value of the lowest node that has both of them in its subtree. A node counts as being in its own subtree, so it can be an ancestor of itself.

example.caption: For 3 and 5, both are bigger than 2 and smaller than 6. Their paths split at 4, so 4 is the answer.

idea.sentence: Walk down from the root: while p and q are both smaller go left, while both are bigger go right, and the first node where they part ways is the answer.

jargon.plain: A tree where everything in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node, and everything in its right subtree is bigger.
The deepest node that sits above (or is) both p and q.

watch.inputHint: Three arguments: the BST as a level-order array, then p, then q (both must be in the tree). e.g. [6,2,8,0,4,7,9,null,null,3,5], 3, 5

compare.bruteLabel: Search the whole tree as if it had no order
compare.optimalLabel: Follow one path down using the BST order
compare.unit: nodes visited, for a balanced tree

rows.name: Plain tree search (ignores order)
rows.note: Works on any binary tree, but looks at nodes it could have skipped.

rows.name: BST walk
rows.note: One step down per level, no recursion. h is about log n when balanced, n when it is a chain.

fast.takeaway: The BST order tells you which side to go, so you never search both. A simple loop with no stack is enough.

stages.title: Start at the root
stages.note: Every common ancestor lies on the path from the root, so begin there.

stages.title: Both smaller: go left
stages.note: If p and q are both smaller than this node, they are both in the left subtree. The answer is in there.

stages.title: Both bigger: go right
stages.note: If p and q are both bigger, they are both in the right subtree. Move right.

stages.title: They split: found it
stages.note: One is on each side, or this node equals one of them. No lower node can hold both, so return this node.

edges.title: One is the ancestor
edges.why: A node can be its own ancestor. At 2, p equals the node, so the condition 'both smaller' fails and we stop.

edges.title: p is the root
edges.why: The very first node already equals p. The walk returns the root.

edges.title: Two-node tree
edges.why: At the root, 1 is smaller and 2 is equal. They are not both smaller, so the root is the answer.

edges.title: p bigger than q
edges.why: The order of p and q does not matter. Each check compares both values to the node.

gotchas.text: Use strict < and >. If a value equals the node, that is a split and the node is the answer. Using <= would walk past it.
This only works on a BST. In a plain binary tree the values give no hint about which side holds them, and you must search both sides.
p and q arrive as numbers, so < and > are correct. If you ever read them from text, convert first: as strings, 10 sorts before 9.
The loop ends with nil only if the values are not in the tree. For valid input it always returns inside the loop.
On a chain-shaped BST the walk takes n steps. The cost is the height, not log n, unless the tree is balanced.

recap.key: Go left while both targets are smaller, right while both are bigger. The first node that is neither is the answer.
